blindSummary:
This country pairs meaningful legal progress with one of the world's highest tolls of violence against transgender people. Twenty-two of its 32 states offer administrative legal gender recognition, the capital and one state have criminalised transfemicide, marriage equality is nationwide, and constitutional anti-discrimination protections exist.

Against that, 71 trans or gender-diverse people were murdered in a single recent year — among the highest national tallies anywhere, with only one other country in its region recording more — with organised crime increasingly involved and impunity near-total. The victims are overwhelmingly local trans women (often sex workers and activists) and migrants in transit, not tourists; violence is also highly concentrated geographically.

In major tourist destinations and the central districts of the capital, heavily policed and progressively governed, a trans visitor's everyday risk is closer to harassment than violence. The dominant hazard for any traveller is the general crime environment. The federal picture is uneven: state-level conditions range from the most protective in the country (the capital) to some of its most dangerous areas.
blindOutOfScope: Organised-crime violence, kidnapping, and theft drive several foreign governments to advise caution or avoidance of non-essential travel for parts of this country — a risk independent of any personal characteristic.
blindSourceSummaries: An international rights group (Mar 2025): assesses trans rights in this country — legal progress and protection, alongside persistent violence and implementation gaps.

International human-rights organisation report (March 2024) on the need for legal gender recognition in one state: murders and violence against trans people (e.g. a trans woman found in a river with a concrete block tied to her feet, Aug 2023) rest on daily discrimination amplified by obstacles to legal name/gender recognition - the mismatch between lived and legal identities leaves trans people exposed.

Foreign broadsheet (July 2024): transfemicide becomes a crime in the capital - a law approved 18 July 2024, a 'watershed' moment named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished.

A newswire report (Jan 2024): a wave of transgender slayings — at least three in the first two weeks of the year, including a well-known activist killed in the capital — sparks anger and street protests by this country's LGBTQ+ community.
Regional human-rights commission press release (2024): expressed concern over violence against trans and gender-diverse people in this country and urged protective measures.
A regional LGBTQ+ news agency (Jun 2024): a data report finds violence against trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the last year in this country.

Academic policy-blog commentary (Nov 2024): LGBTQ+ people in this country face significant threats of violence even as formal rights are extended - analysis of the gap between legal rights and lived safety.
A foreign government's travel advice for this country (updated Aug 2026): 'exercise a high degree of caution' with regional advisories. General travel advice, not trans-specific.

A travel company's country guide: the capital has a large queer scene, an annual Pride and LGBT-friendly venues, plus a beach resort hotspot; the guide notes an indigenous third-gender tradition in the south and advises caution outside tourist hubs.

Foreign-language news channel (July 2024): the capital's legislature approved a law criminalising transfemicide - the second state to do so, after another state did so in March; the law is named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished.

Foreign weekly (Jan 2007): a border state became the third jurisdiction in the region to approve gay civil unions (20-13 vote), following the capital and another regional capital - but the law bars same-sex couples from adopting or getting custody; a governing-party deputy called it 'a sensible response' to discrimination; an opposition party called it 'an attack against the family'.
blindLocalsOnly: The state-by-state administrative legal-gender-recognition regime and the transfemicide statutes (the capital and one state) are resident-facing; the 71-murder toll falls overwhelmingly on local trans women (often sex workers and activists) and migrants in transit.
blindTangential: Marriage equality nationwide — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.
